title: Water or Energy Supply Driven Change in Moisture Availability Switches the Slope Direction Between Shallow Soil Moisture and Actual Evapotranspiration: Interpretation Within the Context of the Complementary Relationship
content:
Abstract

Ecosystem moisture availability (ma) increases as the landscape becomes more energy-limited, driven by either rising water supply or declining energy supply. This study aimed to assess the influence of water and energy supply changes on ma and its effects on actual evapotranspiration (E) and shallow soil moisture (S) dynamics. We simulated the effects of “water-driven” and “energy-driven” changes to ma using the water-energy limits framework combined with the complementary relationship (CR), which considers how ma and sensible heat interact with E and apparent potential evaporation (Epa ${E}_{pa}$). We then compared key hydrological relationships between simulated and observed flux tower data from two sites, where ma variability was predominantly driven by changes in water or energy supply. Additionally, we evaluated whether two CR models, based on the assumption that the Bowen ratio (H/E $H/E$) at equilibrium evaporation is a constant times the Bowen ratio at minimal advection, could reproduce the relationships between observed ma, E, and S at both sites. We found that: (a) the existence of a CR or non-CR between E and Epa ${E}_{pa}$ as a function of ma was determined by whether water supply or energy supply changed more, respectively; (b) the relationship between E and both ma and S switched polarity from positive to negative based on whether water supply or energy supply changed more, respectively; (c) estimating the observed E versus S relationship with a CR model proved more challenging under energy-driven conditions than water-driven conditions; and (d) a CR model utilizing a dynamic form of the Priestley–Taylor α parameter performed best. Our study demonstrated how water and energy supply changes in ma impact key surface energy and water balance variable interactions. To validate CR model results more comprehensively we concluded that researchers should not only utilize observations of E, but also its interaction with ma, and S. Our study demonstrates that a further constraint exists, the slope between S and E, which could be used to better model surface and soil hydrological relationships.
